For winemaker Michael Kouloglou, the decision to move from the mainland to Santorini 11 years ago was a simple one. “It is the mecca of Greek white wine,” he says. Since relocating here from the Athenian Riviera town of Piraeus, he’s worked with a number of local wineries before launching Orycton, his small-batch Assyrtiko featuring grapes grown on old vines from all over the island. It was a winner at the 2023 Decanter World Wine Awards.

On top of the siren’s song of Santorini’s prized volcanic terroir, however, Kouloglou says he appreciates that the region’s windy conditions allow him to pursue his other passions: surfing and kitesurfing.

What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit—when the travelers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing?

If I had to choose the best time to visit, I would choose the entire off-season, from late September until around May. Every part of [offseason] has its own personality: Autumn brings relief after harvest, winter offers complete peace, and spring fills the island with optimism as nature comes back to life, just before the new season begins.
What do you love most about being there during the off-season?

Santorini has two completely different lives. One is the island that millions of visitors experience during summer. The other begins in October and lasts until spring. That is the Santorini only the people who live here truly get to know.

By the end of harvest [in September], both the vineyard and I are exhausted. After weeks of living on adrenaline, my body is desperately asking for rest. Around the end of September, the evenings become cooler; you need a sweater after sunset, the days grow shorter, and the strong summer meltemi (the Aegean wind) gives way to a gentler, northern wind. Everything feels softer. All the locals are tired after another demanding [tourism] season, but at the same time, there is a feeling of optimism. Restaurants and bars begin to close for the season, and that's when the closing parties begin. Friends you haven't seen for months suddenly reappear. You don't even need to make plans; you know you'll see them somewhere during a closing party.

During autumn, you'll still find some travelers, but they are completely different from the summer crowds. They usually come looking for a quieter side of Santorini. They enjoy walking, hiking, discovering wineries and small villages, instead of rushing from one attraction to the next.
By the end of November, even the last seasonal workers have left the island. We have a saying here that the last boat has sailed. From that moment on, Santorini belongs almost entirely to its locals.

This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to winemaker Michael Kouloglou.

For winemaker Michael Kouloglou, the decision to move from the mainland to Santorini 11 years ago was a simple one. “It is the mecca of Greek white wine,” he says. Since relocating here from the Athenian Riviera town of Piraeus, he’s worked with a number of local wineries before launching Orycton, his small-batch Assyrtiko featuring grapes grown on old vines from all over the island. It was a winner at the 2023 Decanter World Wine Awards.

On top of the siren’s song of Santorini’s prized volcanic terroir, however, Kouloglou says he appreciates that the region’s windy conditions allow him to pursue his other passions: surfing and kitesurfing.

Every part of [offseason] has its own personality: Autumn brings relief after harvest, winter offers complete peace, and spring fills the island with optimism as nature comes back to life, just before the new season begins.

What do you love most about being there during the off-season?

Santorini has two completely different lives. One is the island that millions of visitors experience during summer. The other begins in October and lasts until spring. That is the Santorini only the people who live here truly get to know.

By the end of harvest [in September], both the vineyard and I are exhausted. After weeks of living on adrenaline, my body is desperately asking for rest. Around the end of September, the evenings become cooler; you need a sweater after sunset, the days grow shorter, and the strong summer meltemi (the Aegean wind) gives way to a gentler, northern wind. Everything feels softer. All the locals are tired after another demanding [tourism] season, but at the same time, there is a feeling of optimism. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travelers at all?

During autumn, you'll still find some travelers, but they are completely different from the summer crowds. They usually come looking for a quieter side of Santorini. They enjoy walking, hiking, discovering wineries and small villages, instead of rushing from one attraction to the next.

By the end of November, even the last seasonal workers have left the island. We have a saying here that the last boat has sailed. From that moment on, Santorini belongs almost entirely to its locals.
